commercial_incentive: explicit and repeated self-promotion of CollegeVine's blog and consulting services throughout the video
key_insights: MIT does not use the Common App; it uses its own 'MyMIT' system, though much of the biographical information can be copy-pasted directly from a Common App account.
MIT strongly encourages (though does not strictly require) an alumni interview, and the presenter claims the admissions committee gives real weight to interviewer feedback.

At the time of the video, MIT required two teacher evaluations (one math/science, one humanities/social science) plus two SAT Subject Tests (one math, one science) - a requirement since discontinued industry-wide, making this detail dated.

Cites MIT's mid-50% admitted test ranges (SAT verbal 730-780, math 770-800; ACT composite 34-35) and average admitted GPA (4.13 on a 4.3 scale) to argue that meeting minimum stated requirements is not enough given the size of the qualified applicant pool.

Argues MIT extracurricular profiles should show deep, self-motivated 'tinkerer/researcher' involvement in one specific area rather than broad club leadership; illustrates with an example that a deeply researched independent history project outweighs being president of three unrelated clubs.
Claims MIT's early-action admit-rate advantage is unusually small compared to peer schools, contrasting it with Harvard's much larger early-vs-regular admit-rate gap.
specific_numbers_or_facts: MIT class of 2022 cited: ~21,000 applications, ~1,400 admits, ~6.74% overall acceptance rate (stated by presenter)
MIT mid-50% SAT ranges cited: verbal 730-780, math 770-800; ACT composite 34-35; SAT Subject Test target 720+, ideally 780+ (stated by presenter)
Average admitted MIT GPA cited as 4.13 on a 4.3 scale (stated by presenter)
Harvard early admit rate cited as 14.5% vs. 4.59% overall; MIT early admit rate cited as about 6.9% of ~9,500 early applicants, with 6,000+ deferred to regular decision (stated by presenter)
notable_or_distinctive: The specific claim that MIT's early round provides little to no admit-rate boost (unlike most peer schools, illustrated via contrast with Harvard) is a concrete, somewhat unusual data point not commonly highlighted this explicitly.
reliability_notes: Video is 6 years old; MIT has since changed its SAT Subject Test requirement and test-optional policies, so several stated requirements are dated; figures are not cited to a specific source in the transcript, and the video is heavily interspersed with CollegeVine self-promotion.
